newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB opponents to keep battling after barley vote.
newsitem.headline: CWB opponents to keep battling after barley vote.

text.p: Advocates of an open market in barley exports from western Canada vowed on Tuesday to continue their pressure to strip the Canadian Wheat Board of its monopoly on barley exports.

"We're going to press on for dual marketing through lobbying," Western Barley Growers' Association president Buck Spencer told reporters after results of a barley referendum were unveiled by Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale.
Barley growers voted 62.9 percent in favor of keeping the CWB the single-desk exporter for feed and malt barley.

The plebiscite, which registered votes from 57,517 growers or 75 percent of the 77,437 eligible farmers selling grain to the CWB, had been the focus of a bitter dispute centered among Alberta farmers who resent the Board's monopoly power.
Dual marketing would allow farmers a choice to sell to the CWB or private merchants. The CWB opposes dual marketing on grounds it would weaken the CWB's reliability with customers.
About a third of Prairie barley output is exported each year by the CWB. The balance is sold domestically.
Goodale, who ordered the vote, said he would abide by the outcome even though he was not legally bound to do so.

"This does not mean, however, that our overall system of marketing grain can be static or frozen," Goodale said, who noted the vote came as amendments were being proposed to the Canadian Wheat Board Act at the federal level.
CWB's barley export monopoly was attacked when spot prices at U.S. border elevators exceeded CWB monthly offers in 1995.
"We're very, very pleased. We've got nearly 63 percent of farmers supporting the Board," National Farmers Union president Nettie Wiebe said from Regina, Sask.
But in Alberta, where more than 40 percent of Canada's barley is grown, the reaction was swift and sharp.

"A large number of farmers want an open market. But the problems with western Canada's grain marketing system have not been solved with this plebiscite," Alberta Agriculture Minister Walter Paszkowski said.
An Alberta-wide vote in 1995 on the CWB monopoly indicated more than 60 percent of farmers favored open markets.

"It comes down to basic individual rights, it's not about dollars and cents," the Barley Growers' Spencer said. "Over 20,000 farmers voted in favor of open markets and this number is growing every day. Mr. Goodale can't ignore that, and if he does, he's threatening the very existence of the Board."
The Alberta Barley Commission had earlier challenged the CWB's monopoly under Canada's Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Some Canadian farmers trucked wheat and barley to U.S. border elevators in 1995 without CWB export permits. Many have since been convicted under the Canada Customs Act.
"We're going to continue to lobby the government," Western Canadian Wheat Growers president Larry Maguire said of further efforts to address the monopoly.
Votes in favor of keeping the CWB's barley export monopoly totaled 36,170 (62.9 pct). Votes to remove all barley, both feed and malting/food, from the CWB totaled 21,347 (37.1 pct).
